title: 04. OOP: Python Design Patterns & SOLID Principles — Complete Guide
summary: Interview Tip: Design patterns and SOLID are asked in senior interviews. Be ready to explain with real examples, not textbook definitions.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.body: > **Interview Tip:** Design patterns and SOLID are asked in senior interviews. Be ready to explain with real examples, not textbook definitions.

diagrams.title: SOLID at a glance
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  S["S — one reason to change"] --> O["O — extend without editing"]
  O --> L["L — subclasses honour the parent's contract"]
  L --> I["I — small, focused interfaces"]
  I --> D["D — depend on abstractions, inject concrete classes"]
diagrams.explain: The five principles push toward small classes with clear responsibilities, extension through new code instead of edits, substitutable subclasses, narrow interfaces, and dependencies passed in rather than hard-coded. In Python, `Protocol`/ABCs and constructor injection are the usual tools.

sections.title: 1. SOLID Principles

steps.label: S — Single Responsibility Principle (SRP)
steps.narration: A class should have only ONE reason to change.

steps.label: O — Open/Closed Principle (OCP)
steps.narration: Open for extension, closed for modification.

steps.label: L — Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP)
steps.narration: Subtypes must be substitutable for their base types.

steps.label: I — Interface Segregation Principle (ISP)
steps.narration: Don't force clients to depend on interfaces they don't use.

steps.label: D — Dependency Inversion Principle (DIP)
steps.narration: Depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations.

steps.label: 5 Exercises — SOLID

sections.title: 2. Singleton Pattern
sections.body:
**"Ensure a class has only ONE instance."**

### Example 1 — Simple Singleton

```python
class DatabaseConnection:
    _instance = None

    def __new__(cls, *args, **kwargs):
        if cls._instance is None:
            cls._instance = super().__new__(cls)
        return cls._instance

    def __init__(self, host="localhost"):
        # Only initialize once
        if not hasattr(self, '_initialized'):
            self.host = host
            self.connected = False
            self._initialized = True

    def connect(self):
        self.connected = True
        return f"Connected to {self.host}"

db1 = DatabaseConnection("prod-server")
db2 = DatabaseConnection("other-server")  # Returns same instance!
print(db1 is db2)   # True
print(db2.host)      # "prod-server" — not "other-server"
```

### Example 2 — Module-Level Singleton (Pythonic Way)

```python
# config.py — The module itself IS the singleton!
class _Config:
    def __init__(self):
        self.debug = False
        self.database_url = ""

    def load(self, **kwargs):
        for key, value in kwargs.items():
            setattr(self, key, value)

# Module-level instance — created once on first import
config = _Config()

# Usage from other files:
# from config import config
# config.load(debug=True, database_url="postgresql://...")
# print(config.debug)  # True
```

### Example 3 — Singleton Decorator

```python
def singleton(cls):
    instances = {}
    def get_instance(*args, **kwargs):
        if cls not in instances:
            instances[cls] = cls(*args, **kwargs)
        return instances[cls]
    return get_instance

@singleton
class AppConfig:
    def __init__(self):
        self.settings = {}

config1 = AppConfig()
config2 = AppConfig()
print(config1 is config2)  # True
```

### Interview Q&A (3 key questions)

**Q: When should you use Singleton?**

> **A:** Database connections, configuration managers, logging, caches — where exactly one instance makes sense. In Python, module-level instances are the simplest and most Pythonic approach.

**Q: What are the downsides of Singleton?**

> **A:** Global state (hidden dependencies), hard to test (can't easily replace), not thread-safe by default, tight coupling. In Python, prefer module-level instances or dependency injection.

**Q: Is Singleton thread-safe?**

> **A:** The basic implementation is NOT thread-safe. Use `threading.Lock()` to protect instance creation, or initialize at module import time (thread-safe in Python).

sections.title: 3. Factory Pattern
4. Observer Pattern
sections.body:
**"When one object changes, all its dependents are notified."**

### Example 1 — Event System

```python
class EventEmitter:
    def __init__(self):
        self._listeners = {}

    def on(self, event: str, callback):
        """Register a listener for an event."""
        if event not in self._listeners:
            self._listeners[event] = []
        self._listeners[event].append(callback)

    def emit(self, event: str, *args, **kwargs):
        """Notify all listeners of an event."""
        for callback in self._listeners.get(event, []):
            callback(*args, **kwargs)

    def off(self, event: str, callback):
        """Remove a listener."""
        if event in self._listeners:
            self._listeners[event].remove(callback)

# Usage
class OrderService(EventEmitter):
    def place_order(self, order_id, amount):
        # Business logic
        print(f"Order {order_id} placed: ${amount}")
        # Notify listeners
        self.emit("order_placed", order_id=order_id, amount=amount)

# Register listeners
service = OrderService()
service.on("order_placed", lambda **kw: print(f"Email sent for order {kw['order_id']}"))
service.on("order_placed", lambda **kw: print(f"Inventory updated for order {kw['order_id']}"))
service.on("order_placed", lambda **kw: print(f"Analytics logged: ${kw['amount']}"))

service.place_order("ORD-001", 99.99)
# Order ORD-001 placed: $99.99
# Email sent for order ORD-001
# Inventory updated for order ORD-001
# Analytics logged: $99.99
```

sections.title: 5. Strategy Pattern

diagrams.title: Strategy pattern
diagrams.mermaid:
flowchart LR
  ctx["Checkout(pricing=strategy)"] --> iface["PricingStrategy.price(cart)"]
  iface --> r["RegularPricing"]
  iface --> s["SalePricing"]
  iface --> m["MemberPricing"]
diagrams.explain: Strategy moves an interchangeable algorithm behind one interface and injects it, replacing long `if/elif` chains. In Python a strategy is often just a function passed as an argument.

sections.title: 6. Decorator Pattern (OOP, not Python @decorator)
7. Builder Pattern
sections.body:
**"Construct complex objects step by step."**

### Example 1 — Fluent Builder

```python
class QueryBuilder:
    def __init__(self):
        self._table = ""
        self._conditions = []
        self._order_by = ""
        self._limit = None
        self._columns = ["*"]

    def select(self, *columns):
        self._columns = list(columns) if columns else ["*"]
        return self

    def from_table(self, table):
        self._table = table
        return self

    def where(self, condition):
        self._conditions.append(condition)
        return self

    def order_by(self, column, desc=False):
        direction = "DESC" if desc else "ASC"
        self._order_by = f"ORDER BY {column} {direction}"
        return self

    def limit(self, n):
        self._limit = n
        return self

    def build(self):
        columns = ", ".join(self._columns)
        query = f"SELECT {columns} FROM {self._table}"
        if self._conditions:
            query += " WHERE " + " AND ".join(self._conditions)
        if self._order_by:
            query += f" {self._order_by}"
        if self._limit:
            query += f" LIMIT {self._limit}"
        return query

# Fluent interface — read like English
query = (
    QueryBuilder()
    .select("name", "email", "age")
    .from_table("users")
    .where("age > 18")
    .where("active = true")
    .order_by("name")
    .limit(10)
    .build()
)
print(query)
# SELECT name, email, age FROM users WHERE age > 18 AND active = true ORDER BY name ASC LIMIT 10
```

10. Dependency Injection
sections.body:
**"Don't create dependencies inside a class — inject them from outside."**

### Example 1 — Constructor Injection

```python
# BAD — creates its own dependency
class OrderServiceBad:
    def __init__(self):
        self.db = PostgresDatabase()       # Hardcoded!
        self.emailer = SMTPEmailService()  # Hardcoded!
        self.logger = FileLogger()         # Hardcoded!

# GOOD — dependencies are injected
class OrderService:
    def __init__(self, db, emailer, logger):
        self.db = db          # Any database
        self.emailer = emailer  # Any email service
        self.logger = logger    # Any logger

    def place_order(self, order):
        self.db.save(order)
        self.emailer.send(order.customer_email, "Order confirmed!")
        self.logger.log(f"Order {order.id} placed")

# Production
# service = OrderService(PostgresDatabase(), SMTPEmailService(), FileLogger())

# Testing
# service = OrderService(MockDatabase(), MockEmailer(), MockLogger())
```

### Example 2 — Simple DI Container

```python
class Container:
    def __init__(self):
        self._services = {}

    def register(self, name, factory):
        self._services[name] = factory

    def resolve(self, name):
        factory = self._services.get(name)
        if not factory:
            raise KeyError(f"Service '{name}' not registered")
        return factory()

container = Container()
container.register("db", lambda: "PostgresDB instance")
container.register("cache", lambda: "Redis instance")
container.register("user_service", lambda: f"UserService({container.resolve('db')})")

print(container.resolve("user_service"))
```

### 5 Exercises — Design Patterns

1. Implement a Singleton logger that writes to a file.
2. Create a Factory that produces different file parsers (CSV, JSON, XML) based on file extension.
3. Build an Observer-based stock price alert system.
4. Implement Strategy pattern for different discount calculation methods.
5. Create a Builder for constructing HTTP requests with method, URL, headers, and body.

### 7 Interview Questions — Design Patterns

**Q1: What is a design pattern?**

> **A:** A reusable solution to a common software design problem. Not code — it's a template/guideline. Patterns improve communication, reduce complexity, and provide proven solutions.

**Q2: Name the three categories of design patterns.**

> **A:** Creational (Singleton, Factory, Builder) — object creation. Structural (Adapter, Decorator, Facade) — object composition. Behavioral (Observer, Strategy, Command) — object interaction.

**Q3: When is Singleton appropriate?**

> **A:** Database connection pools, configuration managers, logging, caches. When exactly one instance must coordinate actions. In Python, module-level instances are usually simpler.

**Q4: Explain Factory pattern.**

> **A:** Creates objects without exposing creation logic. The client requests an object from the factory, which decides which class to instantiate. Decouples creation from usage.

**Q5: How does Strategy pattern work in Python?**

> **A:** Pass different functions as the strategy — Python's first-class functions make this trivial. `def process(data, strategy=default_strategy):` — swap strategies by passing different functions.

**Q6: What is the difference between Decorator pattern and Python @decorator?**

> **A:** Decorator pattern (OOP): wraps an object to add behavior. Python @decorator: wraps a function/class to modify it. Similar concept, different mechanisms. Python decorators are more flexible.

**Q7: What is Dependency Injection?**

> **A:** Passing dependencies (database, logger, etc.) to a class instead of creating them inside. Enables testing (mock dependencies), flexibility (swap implementations), and follows DIP.

### 8 Scenario-Based Interview Questions — Design Patterns

**S1:** Your application needs to support multiple payment providers. Which pattern?

> **A:** Strategy (swap payment algorithms) + Factory (create the right payment processor based on config). The payment interface defines `charge()` and `refund()`, each provider implements it differently.

**S2:** You're building a notification system that sends via email, SMS, and push. Design it.

> **A:** Factory to create the right notifier, Observer for subscribing to events, Strategy for choosing the notification method. Or simpler: a Notification ABC with Email/SMS/Push implementations + a registry.

**S3:** Your API client needs to add authentication, logging, and retry to every request. Pattern?

> **A:** Decorator pattern: wrap the base client with layers: `RetryDecorator(LoggingDecorator(AuthDecorator(HttpClient())))`. Each layer adds one concern. In Python, function decorators work great here too.

**S4:** Configuration needs to be loaded once and shared everywhere. Singleton or DI?

> **A:** Load config once (module-level or Singleton) and inject it where needed. `config = load_config(); service = Service(config)`. DI makes testing easy — pass different configs.

**S5:** You need to convert between old and new API formats. Pattern?

> **A:** Adapter: wrap the old API to present the new interface. `class OldApiAdapter: def new_method(self): return self.old_api.legacy_method()`. Clean separation.

**S6:** Building complex database queries step by step. Pattern?

> **A:** Builder: `query = QueryBuilder().select("*").from_table("users").where("age > 18").build()`. Fluent interface makes complex construction readable.

**S7:** You want to avoid duplicating business logic across microservices. Approach?

> **A:** Extract shared logic into a library/package. Use Strategy pattern for service-specific behavior. Shared interfaces (Protocols) ensure consistency. Don't share databases.

**S8:** Your class has 15 dependencies in `__init__`. How to manage?

> **A:** Too many dependencies = class does too much (SRP violation). Split into smaller classes. Use a DI container to manage wiring. Group related dependencies into composite objects.

sections.title: Chapter Summary
sections.body:
| Principle/Pattern | Key Takeaway                                          |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- |
| SRP               | One class = one reason to change                      |
| OCP               | Add behavior with new classes, not modifying existing |
| LSP               | Subtypes must work wherever parent types work         |
| ISP               | Many small interfaces > one large interface           |
| DIP               | Depend on abstractions, inject dependencies           |
| Singleton         | One instance — use module-level in Python             |
| Factory           | Create objects without knowing exact types            |
| Observer          | Notify dependents when state changes                  |
| Strategy          | Swap algorithms at runtime (use functions in Python)  |
| Decorator         | Add behavior by wrapping objects                      |
| Builder           | Construct complex objects step by step                |
| Adapter           | Make incompatible interfaces compatible               |
| Repository        | Abstract data access behind an interface              |
| DI                | Pass dependencies, don't create them internally       |
